questions.stem: A 100-mg oral dose of a drug gives an AUC of 20 mg·h/L. A 25-mg IV dose of the same drug gives an AUC of 10 mg·h/L. What is the absolute oral bioavailability?
questions.explanation: F = (AUC_PO/Dose_PO)/(AUC_IV/Dose_IV) = (20/100)/(10/25) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5. A: Compares doses only (25/100). C: Uses AUC_IV/Dose_IV (10/25) alone as F. D: 100% would mean complete absorption; dose-normalized AUCs (0.2 vs 0.4 per mg) show only half is absorbed. E: Ignores the different doses (20/10).

questions.stem: A generic and a brand-name product of the same drug are each given at 500 mg. Their AUCs are 90 and 100 mg·h/L, with similar Cmax. What is the generic's relative bioavailability, and are the products bioequivalent by the 20% rule?

options.D: Can't be determined without an IV dose

questions.explanation: Relative F = (90/500)/(100/500) = 0.90; a 10% difference is within 20%, so they are considered bioequivalent. A: The 10% difference is within the limit. B: Inverts the ratio and misjudges equivalence. C: Confuses the difference with the ratio. D: Relative bioavailability doesn't need an IV reference; absolute does.

questions.stem: A 500-mg IV dose of an antibiotic is given. Its Vd is 30 L and k is 0.2 h⁻¹. Over 48 h, 300 mg are recovered unchanged in urine. What is its renal clearance?
questions.explanation: ClT = k × Vd = 0.2 × 30 = 6 L/h; fe = 300/500 = 0.6; ClR = 6 × 0.6 = 3.6 L/h. A: That's total clearance. B: That's nonrenal clearance (6 − 3.6). C: That's kR (0.2 × 0.6), not a clearance. E: Halves the correct value.

questions.stem: A patient on a continuous IV infusion has a target Css of 20 mg/L and a clearance of 2 L/h. After acute kidney injury, clearance falls to 1 L/h. What infusion rate now maintains the same Css?
questions.explanation: Infusion rate = Css × CL: 40 mg/h before, 20 × 1 = 20 mg/h now. B: Halves the rate twice. C: The old rate, which would double Css. D: Wrongly increases the rate. E: Divides CL by Css.

questions.stem: A patient's daily dose of a drug is split from one large dose into four smaller doses, keeping the same total daily amount. What is the main pharmacokinetic effect?

options.C: Smaller fluctuation between peak and trough concentrations

questions.explanation: More frequent, smaller doses narrow the Cmax–Cmin swing; the average Css depends only on total dose rate, F, and CL. A: The average is unchanged. B: Time to Css depends on half-life, not dosing frequency. D: Half-life is a drug property. E: F doesn't change with dose splitting.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation starts oral digoxin (half-life ≈ 36 h in her) at a fixed daily maintenance dose without a loading dose. When will her digoxin level approach steady state?

options.E: Never, because digoxin follows zero-order kinetics

questions.explanation: Steady state takes ~4–5 half-lives: 4–5 × 36 h ≈ 6–7.5 days. A: One half-life gives only 50% of Css. B: ~2 half-lives gives ~75%. C: Far longer than 5 half-lives. E: Digoxin follows first-order kinetics at therapeutic doses.
questions.source: Quantitative PK, slide 37; PK Problem Solving, solution 2c

questions.stem: A 400-mg oral dose of a drug (F = 0.5) is given. Total clearance is 10 L/h. Over 48 h, 100 mg of unchanged drug is recovered in the urine. What is the renal clearance?
questions.explanation: Only the absorbed dose (0.5 × 400 = 200 mg) reaches the circulation, so the fraction excreted unchanged = 100/200 = 0.5 and ClR = 0.5 × 10 = 5 L/h. A: Uses 100/400, ignoring F. B: That's total clearance. D: Nonrenal clearance from the uncorrected fraction (10 − 2.5). E: Divides total clearance by F.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient takes a drug with a Vd of 100 mL/kg and a half-life of 3.5 h (first-order). Taking 0.693 ≈ 0.7, what is its total body clearance?
questions.explanation: Vd = 0.1 L/kg × 70 kg = 7 L; k = 0.7/3.5 = 0.2 h⁻¹; CL = k × Vd = 0.2 × 7 = 1.4 L/h. A: A 10× error in the mL→L conversion. B: Omits 0.693 (7/3.5). C: Divides Vd by k instead of multiplying. D: Forgets to multiply by body weight (0.1 × 0.2).
